column2: Rushadgu, Kavasa, Dhaumya, the mighty Parivyadha, Ekata, Dvita and Trita, great sages,
and the blessed son of Atri and the lord Sarasvata: these nine great souls rest in the western quarter.
Atreya, Vasishtha and the great sage Kashyapa, Gautama with Bharadvaja, Vishvamitra and Kaushika,
and likewise the blessed son of the great-souled Richika, Jamadagni: these seven rest in the northern quarter.
These, of keen splendour, are all named for each direction, great souls, witnesses, makers of the worlds.
Thus these great souls stand each in a direction; by reciting them one is freed from all sins.
He who takes refuge in whichever direction these dwell is freed from all sins and may go home in safety."
[Yudhishthira said:] "And his great radiance and his ancient deed, tell me all of it as it truly is, bull of the Bharatas.
How did Hari take on a form born of an animal womb? For what purpose of creation? Tell me that, grandsire."
[Bhishma said:] "Long ago I went hunting and stayed at Markandeya's hermitage; there I saw thousands of sages sitting together.
Then they honoured me with madhuparka, and having accepted that honour I greeted the sages.
This tale was told there by the great sage Kashyapa, a divine one that gladdens the mind; hear it here, one-pointed.
Long ago, the foremost Danavas, joined with anger and greed, drunk with strength, hundreds of them, Naraka and other great asuras,
and many other Danavas, intoxicated with battle, could not bear that unsurpassed prosperity of the gods.
Oppressed by the Danavas, the gods and divine sages found no peace, king, entering here and there.
The bewildered will not understand Vishnu, whose appearance is unmanifest, the god in boar form, unassailable even by the immortals.
He will go with speed to where those lowest Danavas live in thousands, dreadful, gone beneath the earth, and will pacify them." Hearing this, the best of the gods rejoiced.
Then Vishnu of great splendour, taking the boar form, entered beneath the earth and went toward the sons of Aditi's rivals.
Seeing a superhuman being, all the Daityas together rushed, bewildered by Time, and stood up suddenly.
All rushing together seized the boar, and enraged, dragged the boar on every side.
The great lords of the Danavas, huge-bodied, of great valour, swollen with strength, could do nothing to him then, lord.
Then those Danava lords fell into astonishment from fear, and thought themselves, by thousands, in doubt.
Then the god of gods, self of yoga, charioteer of yoga, the blessed one, resorting to yoga, best of the Bharatas,
let out a great roar, agitating the Daityas and Danavas; by it all the worlds and all ten directions resounded.
By that roaring sound the worlds were shaken, and all the directions were confused, and the gods led by Shakra.
The world too became utterly motionless then, the unmoving and moving alike bewildered by that roar.
Then all those Danavas, terrified by that sound, fell lifeless, bewildered by Vishnu's splendour.
And the Boar tore with his hooves the enemies of the gods who had gone to the nether world, heaps of flesh, fat and bone.
By that great roar he is remembered as Sanatana, the lotus-naveled, the great yogi, teacher of beings, lord of beings.
Then all hosts of gods said to the Grandfather: "What kind of sound is this, god? We do not know it, lord; who is that, or whose sound is it, by which the world is troubled?"
Meanwhile Vishnu, in boar form, rose up, great god, praised by great sages.
[The Grandfather said:] "Having slain the lords of the Danavas, this great-bodied, mighty god, the great yogi, self of beings, maker of beings,
lord of all beings, yogi, the source and self of the self: let this Krishna, destroyer of all sins, be steady.
Having done this very good deed, impossible, the immeasurable lord has come to his own self, greatly fortunate, greatly radiant, lotus-naveled, great yogi, self of beings, maker of beings.
Neither distress nor fear nor grief should be felt, best of gods; this is ordinance and his power, Time the cause of destruction. This sound was uttered by that great soul as he bears the worlds."
He indeed, greatly fortunate, saluted by all worlds, Achyuta, lotus-eyed, is the source of all beings."
[Bhishma said:] "Here too they cite this ancient tale, a dialogue joined with liberation, of a disciple with his teacher.
A certain disciple, very wise, seeking the good, well collected, approaching a brahmana teacher, best of sages, who sat, clasped his feet and, standing with folded hands, said:

If, blessed one, you are pleased with my service, I have a great doubt; you should explain it to me.
mahabharata:12:203.5	Whence am I, and whence are you? Tell me rightly what is supreme. And how is it, best of the twice-born, that among all beings, equal, those who conduct themselves rightly turn back, with the opposites of decay and rise?
mahabharata:12:203.6	And the word that is in the Vedas, worldly and pervasive: this, learned one, you should explain in truth, all of it.
[The teacher said:] "Hear, disciple of great wisdom, this supreme secret of Brahman, the self of all beings, and the wealth of the scriptures.
Vasudeva is all this, the mouth of Brahman of the universe; he is truth, giving, sacrifice, forbearance, self-control and honesty.
That eternal Person, Vishnu, whom the knowers of the Veda know, the creator and dissolver, unmanifest, eternal Brahman: hear from me this Brahman, this tale of the Vrishni."
Ancestors, gods and sages, likewise yakshas and Danavas, nagas, asuras and men, the supreme imperishable creates.
So also the Vedas, the shastras and the eternal dharmas of the world: at dissolution, reaching nature, the lord creates them at the beginning of the age.
As in the seasons the marks of the seasons are seen in manifold forms in turn, those same ones, so too Brahma in days and nights.
Then whatever is to be, at whatever time, from the union of time, at the beginning of ages, that knowledge arises, born of the ordering of the course of the world.
At the end of the age the Vedas with the histories disappeared; the great sages obtained them again through austerity, permitted by the Self-born.
The blessed Brihaspati knew the Veda and the limbs of the Veda; Bhargava taught the science of policy for the good of the world.
Narada taught the Gandharva Veda; Bharadvaja the grasp of the bow; Garga the conduct of the divine sages; Krishnatreya medicine.
Many systems of reasoning were spoken by those and those disputants; what is said by reasons, scripture and good conduct is followed.
The supreme Brahman, which is without beginning, neither gods nor sages know; the blessed Narayana, the lord, the Creator, alone knows it.
From Narayana the hosts of sages, the chiefs, the gods and asuras, the royal sages and the ancients come, the supreme remedy for sorrow.
Nature brings forth the thing supervised by the Person, and then, joined with its cause, the whole world revolves.
As other lamps are lit by thousands from one lamp, so nature creates, and by its endlessness is not diminished.
Intellect, born of unmanifest action, brings forth ego; from ego, space; from space, wind arose.
From wind, fire; then water; from water the earth emerged; these are the eight root natures, and the world rests in them.
Then the five senses of knowledge and the five senses of action, the five objects, and in modification the mind as sixteenth.
Ear, skin, the two eyes, tongue and nose are the five senses; the feet, the anus, the generative organ, the hands and speech are for the senses of action.
Sound, touch, form, taste and smell are the objects; thought is pervasive, and the mind goes through them all.
The tongue is for knowing taste, and speech for utterance; all things are scattered, joined with various senses, and so is the mind.
Know these sixteen as deities in their divisions; in bodies they worship the one who knows and acts, who is seated.
So the tongue has the quality of Soma, smell is the quality of earth, hearing has the quality of sound and the eye the quality of fire; touch know as the quality of wind in all beings always.
They say mind has the quality of sattva, and sattva is born of the unmanifest; dwelling as the self of all beings, so the wise should know it.
These states carry the whole world, moving and unmoving; the god free of rajas, whom they call the supreme state, is resorted to.
The holy city of nine gates, joined with these states, is pervaded and lain in by the great self; therefore he is called Purusha.
He is unageing and immortal, instructive of the manifest and unmanifest, pervasive, with qualities, subtle, the support of the qualities of all beings.
As a lamp, whose nature is light, is small or great, so know the Person, whose nature is knowledge, in all creatures.
He here knows the knowable, he hears, he sees; this body is his instrument; he is the doer of all actions.
As fire in wood is not seen when the wood is split, so the self in the body is seen here only by yoga.
As waters join in rivers, as rays go with the sun, spreading, so go the bodies of the embodied.
As in dream-yoga the self, joined with the five senses, leaves the body and goes, so it is found here.
He is pervaded by action first, and arises by action, and is led elsewhere by action, by the stronger of his own making.
As he, leaving one body, takes up another, so I shall tell you of this host of beings born of its own actions."
[The teacher said:] "As the great tree contained in the fig-seed is seen clearly when it has come forth, so there is origin from the unmanifest.
As the lifeless iron rushes to the magnet, both without consciousness, and like things born of their own nature and cause,
so states born of the unmanifest bear the marks of the doer and the cause; the unconscious are joined by the cause of the conscious one.
Neither earth, sky, heaven, beings, sages nor gods and asuras; there was nothing else but the living soul; they did not come together.
By all policy, the pervasive great, marked by its cause, is indicated by ignorance and action; this is the mark of the cause.
That, joined with causes, produces the collection of effects, by which this great wheel without beginning or end turns.
The wheel with the unmanifest as its nave, the manifest as its maker, and the circle of modifications, supervised by the knower of the field, with oily axle, turns firmly.
Because of the oil, all the world is crushed on this wheel like sesame, pressed by enjoyments born of ignorance as by oil-presses.
As wind may be dusty or dustless, so the wise should know this difference between the field and the knower of the field. By practice, thus joined, he does not return to nature again.
The blessed sage cut this doubt that had arisen; likewise one should look at the matter as measured by the marks made.
As seeds burnt by fire do not sprout again, so the self is not bound again by afflictions burnt by knowledge."
[The teacher said:] "Rare are the knowers of the Veda who stand in what the Veda says; therefore they seek here the praised path for the purpose.
Because it has been practised by the good, this conduct is not blamed; there is this understanding and another, by which one goes to the supreme goal.
The embodied one through delusion takes up all possessions, joined with states such as desire and anger, rajasic and tamasic.
Therefore one should not do the impure, wishing to maintain the body; making a gap in action, he would not gain the good worlds.
As gold joined with alloy and not well refined does not shine, so knowledge called unripe in its astringency does not shine.
He who through delusion practises adharma, following desire and greed, having left the righteous path, perishes with his followers.
Therefore one should follow the objects of sound and the rest without attachment; anger, joy and despondency arise from each other.
In a body of five elements, with sattva, rajas and tamas, whom does this one praise, or whom shout at, or what should he say?
So, in the wilderness of the world, intent on toil, one should take food for the journey, as a sick man takes medicine.
With truth, purity, honesty and renunciation, with fame and valour, forbearance, steadiness, intellect, mind and austerity alone,
he should live with all states as they come, in order; wishing peace, with undismayed self, he should restrain the senses.
Bewildered by sattva, rajas and tamas, creatures revolve like a wheel greatly, from ignorance.
Therefore one should examine well the faults born of ignorance, and always give up ego, born of ignorance.
The great elements, the senses, the qualities, sattva, rajas and tamas: the three worlds with their lord, all, are founded on ego.
As time here shows the fixed qualities of the seasons, so know ego among beings as the mover of beings.
Know tamas as the bewilderer, dark, born of ignorance; and the three qualities all bound with joy and sorrow: learn them, of sattva, rajas and tamas.
Delusion, joy-born delight, freedom from doubt, steadiness, memory: know these as the qualities of sattva; these others are rajasic and tamasic.
Desire, anger, heedlessness, greed, delusion, fear, weariness, despondency, grief, discontent, pride, arrogance and ignobleness,
of such faults as these, examining the heavy and light, one should consider each in turn, those resting in oneself."
[The disciple said:] "Which faults are given up by the mind, which loosened by the intellect? Which come again and again, which are fruitless from delusion?
Of which should the wise man weigh strength and weakness by reasons and intellect? Tell me all this, lord, so that I may know."
[The teacher said:] "With faults cut off from the root, the pure soul is freed; as an iron one destroys what has arisen, so the self-trained one is destroyed by innate rajasic faults.
Rajasic and tamasic, born of the action of the pure-souled, all that is the seed of embodied beings; all is the same for the self-possessed.
Therefore the self-possessed should avoid rajas and tamas; freed from rajas and tamas, sattva would become spotless.
Or they say, with mantras, of eaters of meat, the Yajus is made; the same is the reason in abstaining from taking and in keeping to pure dharma.
By rajas he undertakes tasks joined with dharma and wealth, and excessively enjoys all desires.
By tamas he pursues what is joined with greed and born of anger, delighting in violence, drowsy and sleepy.
Abiding in sattva, resorting to it, he sees pure sattvic states; that embodied one is spotless, fortunate, pure, endowed with knowledge."
[The teacher said:] "They enter the supreme Self, the god, imperishable and undecaying, Vishnu, established in the unmanifest, best of gods.
Men, their limbs pierced by his maya, fallen from knowledge and without hope, from the bewilderment of knowledge then go to desire.
From desire they reach anger, and greed and delusion; from pride and arrogance, ego; from ego, actions.
From actions come the bond of affection; from affection, grief; from the beginning of pleasure and pain, births and non-births, moments made.
From birth, the dwelling in the womb, born of semen and blood, and turbid with the origin of excrement, urine, moisture and blood.
Overcome by craving, bound by them, floating among them, there one should understand women as the carriers of the web of the world.
By nature they are the field; men are marked as the knower of the field; therefore the wise man should especially pass beyond them.
These are the witches in dreadful form who bewilder the unwise; the eternal form of the senses is concealed in rajas.
Rajas is cast in tamas; sattva stands in tamas; ignorance is the seat of knowledge, marked by intellect and ego.
They call that the seed of the embodied, that seed called the soul; by action joined with time it turns the cycle of the world.
As the embodied one, as in dream, seems to delight in a body with the mind, so, with qualities carrying the womb of action, he comes to be in the womb.
Impelled by action as seed, whichever sense it is arises from ego, with a mind joined with attachment.
From attachment to sound the ear is born for him of purified self; from attachment to form, the eye; the nose from the wish for scent.
From touches, the wind, dependent on prana and apana; vyana, udana and samana: the fivefold support of the body.
By limbs that are born, produced by action, covered by Brahma, a man is of sorrow at its beginning, middle and end, bodily and mental.
Know sorrow from taking up, and it grows from conceit; by giving up those, there is cessation; the knower of cessation is freed.
Of the senses both rise and dissolution are in rajas alone; the wise man should move about, examining with the eye of scripture.
The senses of knowledge do not approach the objects of the senses eagerly; by the causes known, the embodied one does not deserve a body again."
[The teacher said:] "Among all beings the Person is said to be the best; above persons they place the twice-born; above the twice-born, those who speak mantras.
They are distinguished among all beings, omniscient, all-seeing, the brahmanas who know the truth of the Veda, resolved on the truth of the purpose.
As a blind man meets hardship on the road, so the man without knowledge in the world; therefore the knowers of knowledge are superior.
Those wishing for dharma follow these and those dharmas according to scripture; but there is no common wealth for them apart from these virtues.
Purity of speech, body and mind, forbearance, truth, steadiness, memory: knowers of dharma teach these virtues in all dharmas.
That form of Brahman which is held to be celibacy is supreme above all beings; by it they go to the supreme goal.
That which is free of union with the mark and free of touch of the body, hearing by the ear, seeing by the eye,
tasting by the tongue, that too is given up; with intellect and resolve, celibacy is without stain.
Celibacy is very hard; hear from me the means: the twice-born should restrain the mind when it has arisen and risen.
Tales of women should not be heard, nor naked women be looked at; by sometimes seeing them, passion enters the weak.
When passion arises, he should practise austerity, enter water thrice a day; if overcome in a dream, he should mentally mutter the Aghamarshana three times.
Thus the wise man should burn up the sin, the rajas-made, within, with a mind joined with knowledge, continually.
As a bond without gap joined with filth and impurity, so know the self in the body as bound by the body.
Wind, bile and phlegm, blood, skin, flesh, sinew, bone and marrow, the juices of men nourish through the net of veins.
Ten channels here carry the qualities of the five senses; by them the other subtle channels, thousands, are extended.
So these veins are rivers carrying juice and nourish the ocean of the body in due time, as rivers the ocean.
In the middle of the heart there is one vein, the mind-carrying one; it sends out in all limbs the semen born of the intention of men.
The veins that spread through all the limbs, following it, reach the eyes, carrying the quality of fire.
As ghee hidden in milk is churned out with a churning-stick, so semen is churned out by the churning sticks born of the body's intention.
So too in dream the mind-born passion arrives, and the mind-carrying vein sends out semen, untouched, from the body of the man.
The great sage, the blessed Atri, knew the origin of that semen; it has three seeds, its deity is Indra; therefore it is called indriya.
Those who know the course of semen, which causes mixing of beings, are detached, their faults burnt, and do not gain birth in a body.
Having reached equality of the qualities, with mind alone driving the mind, impelling the breaths of bodily action, he is freed at the end of time.
Knowledge will come from the mind, the mind itself is extended; the luminous, stainless, divine is perfected here for the great souls.
Therefore, to avoid harm to it, one should do stainless action; having given up rajas and tamas here, he would not reach an animal birth.
Knowledge gained in youth becomes weak by paramours; but with ripe understanding, in time, one takes up mental strength.
Having crossed beyond the bond of qualities, as a very hard road, when he sees, then passing beyond faults, he enjoys immortality."
[The teacher said:] "Seeing this world ever beset by birth, death, old age, sorrow, disease and mental weariness, the wise should strive for liberation.
Pure in speech, mind and body, without ego, calm, knowing, a mendicant should wander happily, without expectation.
Or he should see attachment of the mind out of compassion for beings; even there he should be indifferent, knowing the world as the fruit of action.
Whatever good or evil deed was done before he enjoys; therefore one should do good deeds by speech, mind and action.
Non-violence, truthful speech, honesty toward all beings, forbearance and heedfulness: he who has these will be happy.
He who knows this supreme dharma, bringing happiness to all beings and the way out of sorrow, is a knower of truth and will be happy.
Therefore he should hold the mind collected by intellect on beings; he should not wish ill, nor crave, nor think of the unreal, unbound.
By the practice of silent yoga the knowing mind goes forth; or wishing to speak, regarding subtle dharma, he should speak true, non-violent, unslanderous speech.
As a flock of sheep scattered would be driven by robbers, so the unwise, knowing the world to be contrary, are driven.
And as, having thrown off those same robbers, one goes to the auspicious quarter, so, leaving rajasic and tamasic actions, one gains happiness.
Free of doubt, without effort, freed from all possessions, living in solitude, light of diet, an ascetic of restrained senses,
with afflictions burnt by knowledge, delighting in practice, self-possessed, with a mind free of wandering, he reaches that supreme.
The steady, self-possessed one should restrain the intellect without doubt; he should restrain the mind by intellect, and the objects by the mind of himself.
When his senses are restrained and he holds the mind in control, those deities appear and, delighted, go to that lord.
With a mind attached to them, he shines like Brahman; by the loss of all these he becomes fit for Brahman.
Or he should not engage but set about by the rules of yoga; by whatever system, let his livelihood be such and he should practise that.
Grains, oil-cake, thick gruel, vegetables, barley, meal, roots, fruit, and alms, he should take in turn.
Diet restrained, in place and time sattvic: examining that, he should follow what supports his activity.
He should not suppress activity but slowly kindle it like fire; then knowledge, kindled by knowledge, shines like the sun.
Ignorance is the seat of knowledge, and rules the three worlds; knowledge accompanied by discernment is drawn away by ignorance.
Because of separateness and of association, they do not envy the eternal Veda; the knower of the release from both, free of attachment, is freed.
Past the age, conquering old age and death, he gains the eternal Brahman, the immortal, the imperishable, undecaying."
[The disciple said:] "In dream the embodied one is overcome by rajas and tamas; as if gone into another body, he moves with memory gone.
By the practice of knowledge, in waking, for inquiry, afterwards, by the devotion of discernment, he wakes ever and always.
Now what is this state, in dream, as if with objects? With senses merged, the embodied one acts as if with a body."
[The teacher said:] "Here it is said, as Hari, lord of yogis, knows it; so the great sages describe it, with its meaning established.
The wise say dream comes from the fatigue of the senses and is all-pervasive; and from the mind's absorption they give that example.
As the intention of one waking whose mind is engrossed in tasks, so the lordship of wishes in dream is in the mind.
The desire-natured one may gain this in countless worlds; all that is hidden in the mind that excellent Person knows.
Whatever action of the qualities comes to hand, he knows; and beings praise that as the mind has been formed.
That which is being and non-being and the unmanifest sleeps; here is the example; they know it as the quality of the self, dwelling as the self of all beings.
He who by mind desires the lordly quality through intention should be known by the power of the self; for all the deities are in the self.
So, joined with austerity, like the sun beyond darkness, the embodied one, the nature of the three worlds, by austerity reaches the Great Lord.
Austerity is supported by the gods; darkness, a mass, by the asuras; this, guarded by gods and asuras, they say is marked by knowledge.
They know sattva, rajas and tamas as the qualities of gods and asuras; know sattva as the quality of the gods, the other two as asuric.
That supreme Brahman, the knowable, immortal, light, imperishable: those self-trained ones who know it go to the supreme goal.
So much can be said with reasoning to the eye of knowledge; or by withdrawal the unmanifest Brahman can be known."
[The teacher said:] "Know the manifest as the mouth of death and the unmanifest as the immortal state; the sage Narayana spoke of the dharma marked by activity.
In this alone all three worlds, moving and unmoving, are situated; the dharma marked by withdrawal is the unmanifest, eternal Brahman.
Prajapati then spoke the dharma marked by activity: activity is return, withdrawal is the highest goal.
The sage devoted to withdrawal reaches that supreme goal, ever intent on the truth of knowledge, pointing out the good and bad."
Generous, of sweet speech, free of envy, master of his senses, righteous-souled, merciful, valorous and not boastful.
Constantly oppressed by his elder brother, Bharata, he gave up his wealth, took to the directions as his clothing, and chose to live in the forest.
You are our father, you are our mother, you are our supreme teacher; deprived of you, where shall we stay?
Sons killed fathers and fathers sons, Bharata; intoxicated, they rushed about striking one another.
Mounting that chariot, the king, bull of the Kuru line, quickly rose upward, filling heaven and earth with his splendour.
He who has done mostly sinful deeds first attains heaven; by that I have led you so, wishing your good, king.
